Methanol toxicity

In methanol-intoxicated rats, 670 nm LED treatment reduced retinal histopathology and improved rod- and cone-mediated function compared with untreated animals. Human efficacy is untested.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In methanol-intoxicated rats, 670 nm LED treatment reduced retinal histopathology and improved rod- and cone-mediated function compared with untreated animals. Human efficacy is untested.

Summary of the Evidence

One 2003 publication is mapped to methanol-induced retinal toxicity. It is a rat experiment, with no human clinical report, animal replication, or separate cell study listed in this indication. The outcome is retinal function and pathology after experimentally induced methanol intoxication, not treatment of human poisoning. Eells et al. 2003

Human and clinical evidence

No human PBM study in methanol toxicity was identified. The experiment does not assess clinical management, systemic complications, or long-term visual recovery in patients. Treatment in a controlled animal setting cannot be used to infer the safety or effectiveness of light exposure during human methanol poisoning.

Animal evidence

In a rat model, methanol-derived formate disrupted retinal structure and rod- and cone-mediated function. Eells et al. reported that 670 nm LED treatment attenuated histopathological retinal damage and improved electroretinographic function compared with untreated intoxicated animals. Functional recovery was not fully equivalent to uninjured controls across all measures. The report supports a protective or restorative signal in this model, but it remains one experiment.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate in-vitro or ex-vivo methanol-toxicity study was listed for this indication.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The publication used 670 nm LED exposure after methanol intoxication, with repeated post-insult treatment described in the study record. The source does not provide a validated patient dose. Animal eye exposure, systemic toxicant kinetics, and timing differ from clinical poisoning care.

Interpretation

The experiment suggests retinal function can be modified by red-light treatment in one rat model of methanol toxicity. It does not establish a human treatment, the optimal intervention window, or whether a similar exposure is safe alongside emergency medical care. Clinical claims are unsupported.

Evidence strength in source summaryRetinal function after methanol toxicity: One rat-model signal Human toxicity outcomes: No direct evidence
Publications and records1 publication: 1 controlled rat experiment.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Evidence is one controlled rat experiment. Treatment attenuated formate-associated retinal pathology and improved rod- and cone-mediated function, but the study does not demonstrate full normalization or any clinical effect in people with methanol poisoning. The treatment window and optimal dose are undetermined.

Publication and study types

  • No human cohort or clinical trial, independent animal replication, or separate in-vitro or ex-vivo study is listed for methanol-induced retinal toxicity.
